title: Female reproductive system and the menstrual cycle
blurb: Follow the oocyte from ovary to uterus, link each phase of the 28-day cycle to its hormones, and explain hCG, oxytocin and prolactin in pregnancy and lactation.
question: A patient with a regular 28-day cycle asks why her period starts about two weeks after ovulation unless she becomes pregnant. Which structure and hormone keep the uterine lining in place, and what makes a pregnancy test turn positive?

teach.body: The ovaries produce oocytes (oogenesis) and the hormones estrogen and progesterone. The uterine (fallopian) tubes catch the ovulated oocyte and are where fertilization usually happens. The uterus houses the developing embryo; its lower neck, the cervix, opens into the vagina, which is the birth canal and the outlet for menstrual flow. The vulva is the external genitalia, and the mammary glands are accessory organs that produce milk.

steps.sub: Sweep the oocyte into the tube

steps.label: Along the tube
steps.sub: Cilia and peristalsis move the embryo

teach.caption: An ectopic pregnancy is implantation outside the uterus, usually in the uterine tube.
Note the ovary is not joined to the tube: the fimbriae sweep the released oocyte in. Fertilization usually happens in the tube.

teach.h: The three layers of the uterus
teach.caption: Only the functional layer of the endometrium is shed in menstruation.

teach.h: Oogenesis: a process with long pauses
teach.body: Oogenesis begins before birth. Primary oocytes stop (arrest) in prophase I until puberty. Each cycle, one completes meiosis I just before ovulation, forming a secondary oocyte and a first polar body. Meiosis II is completed only if fertilization occurs. One oogonium yields one ovum plus polar bodies, while one spermatocyte yields four sperm. The egg always carries an X chromosome.

teach.caption: High estrogen from the growing follicle is what triggers the LH surge.
When progesterone falls, the functional endometrium is shed and day 1 comes around again.

teach.body: About 6-7 days after fertilization, the blastocyst implants. Its trophoblast (the future placenta) secretes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum alive; hCG is what pregnancy tests detect. Progesterone maintains the endometrium and relaxes the myometrium. In labor, oxytocin drives contractions (positive feedback). After birth, prolactin makes milk and oxytocin ejects it (let-down). At menopause, follicles run out: estrogen and progesterone fall, FSH and LH rise.

Leah has a 28-day cycle. Around day 14 an LH surge triggers ovulation, and the oocyte is fertilized in the ampulla of a uterine tube. About a week later the blastocyst implants in her endometrium, and its trophoblast secretes hCG. hCG keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone, so her lining is not shed and her period does not come. Her home test turns positive because it detects hCG.

teach.text: The LH surge, not FSH, causes ovulation. The corpus luteum secretes mainly PROGESTERONE. hCG comes from the embryo's trophoblast, not the mother's pituitary. Prolactin PRODUCES milk; oxytocin EJECTS it. Fertilization happens in the uterine tube, not the uterus.

items: Fertilization: ampulla of the uterine tube; implantation: the endometrium.
Myometrium = smooth muscle that contracts in labor; functional endometrium is shed.
FSH grows follicles, estrogen rises, the LH surge triggers ovulation around day 14.
Corpus luteum secretes progesterone; it degenerates without hCG, causing menstruation.
Meiosis II finishes only after fertilization; prolactin makes milk, oxytocin ejects it.

summary: You can now trace the oocyte from ovary to implantation, name the uterine layers and match each phase of the 28-day cycle to its hormones. You can also explain how hCG maintains a pregnancy and which hormones drive labor, milk production and milk ejection.

A.why: The sperm usually meets the secondary oocyte in the ampulla, the wide outer part of the uterine (fallopian) tube.

whyNot.0: The oocyte is released from the ovary at ovulation; fertilization happens after it enters the tube.
whyNot.2: The endometrium is where the blastocyst implants, about a week after fertilization.
whyNot.3: The cervix is the passage sperm swim through, not the usual site of fertilization.

A.q: Which hormone surge directly triggers ovulation?
A.why: A surge of luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary causes the dominant follicle to release its oocyte.

whyNot.0: FSH stimulates follicles to grow but does not trigger ovulation.
whyNot.1: High estrogen triggers the LH surge, but LH is the hormone that causes ovulation.
whyNot.3: Progesterone rises after ovulation, from the corpus luteum.

A.q: Which part of the uterus is shed during menstruation?
A.why: When progesterone falls, the functional layer of the endometrium breaks down and is shed as menstrual flow.

whyNot.1: The myometrium is the muscular layer that contracts; it is not shed.
whyNot.2: The perimetrium is the outer covering of the uterus; it is not shed.
whyNot.3: The cervix is the neck of the uterus; its lining is not what is shed each month.

B.q: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum. Which hormone does it MAINLY secrete?
B.why: The corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone (with some estrogen), which drives the secretory phase.

whyNot.0: FSH comes from the anterior pituitary and stimulates follicle growth.
whyNot.1: hCG is made by the embryo's trophoblast; it keeps the corpus luteum alive but is not secreted by it.
whyNot.2: Prolactin comes from the anterior pituitary and drives milk production.

B.q: Which statement about the uterine cycle is CORRECT?
options: The endometrium is thinnest in the secretory phase
The secretory phase is driven by progesterone
B.why: After ovulation, progesterone from the corpus luteum makes the endometrium thicken and its glands secrete.

whyNot.0: The proliferative phase follows menstruation and comes before ovulation.
whyNot.1: Menstruation begins when progesterone falls, as the corpus luteum degenerates.
whyNot.2: The lining is thickest in the secretory phase; it is thinnest just after menstruation.

B.q: A home pregnancy test detects which hormone?
B.why: The embryo's trophoblast secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) after implantation; pregnancy tests detect it.

whyNot.1: LH peaks at ovulation in every cycle, pregnant or not.
whyNot.2: Progesterone rises after every ovulation, so it does not confirm pregnancy.
whyNot.3: Estrogen rises in every follicular phase, so it does not confirm pregnancy.

C.q: A new mother's milk lets down each time her baby starts to nurse. Which statement about the hormones of lactation is CORRECT?
options: Prolactin ejects milk; oxytocin produces it
Prolactin ejects milk; progesterone produces it
Oxytocin ejects milk; prolactin produces it
Oxytocin ejects milk; estrogen produces it
C.why: Prolactin (anterior pituitary) drives milk production; oxytocin (posterior pituitary) causes milk ejection, or let-down.

whyNot.0: This reverses the two hormones' roles.
whyNot.1: Prolactin produces milk rather than ejecting it, and progesterone does not produce milk.
whyNot.3: Oxytocin does eject milk, but prolactin, not estrogen, produces it.

C.q: Leah has a regular 28-day cycle and is not pregnant. Which event is MOST likely on about day 14?
C.why: In a typical 28-day cycle, the LH surge triggers ovulation at about day 14.

whyNot.0: Without a pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates around days 22-24, well after ovulation.
whyNot.2: The functional endometrium is shed on days 1-5.
whyNot.3: hCG appears only after implantation in a pregnancy, which Leah does not have.

C.q: Which statement about oogenesis is CORRECT?
options: Meiosis II is completed only if fertilization occurs
Meiosis II is completed just before ovulation occurs
Each oogonium produces four functional egg cells
Oogenesis begins at puberty, just as spermatogenesis does
C.why: The ovulated secondary oocyte is arrested in meiosis II and finishes it only when a sperm fertilizes it.

whyNot.1: Meiosis I is completed just before ovulation; meiosis II waits for fertilization.
whyNot.2: One oogonium produces one ovum plus polar bodies; four gametes is the sperm pattern.
whyNot.3: Oogenesis begins before birth, with primary oocytes arrested in prophase I until puberty.

reteach.title: Think of a hotel room made up every month
reteach.question: A hotel makes up a room every month for a guest who may or may not arrive. How does that match the uterine lining, the corpus luteum and hCG?

blocks.h: Ready the room, then wait for a call
blocks.body: Each month the uterus makes up a room: the endometrium rebuilds (proliferative) and is furnished (secretory). The corpus luteum is the housekeeper who keeps the room ready by supplying progesterone. If a guest checks in (a blastocyst implants), it phones the front desk with hCG, telling the housekeeper to stay. If no guest arrives, the housekeeper leaves, progesterone falls and the room is stripped: menstruation.

blocks.text: The guest (embryo) makes the phone call: hCG comes from the trophoblast, not from the mother's pituitary or ovary.

explain.body: Ovaries make oocytes and hormones; fimbriae sweep the oocyte into the uterine tube; fertilization in the ampulla; implantation in the endometrium; myometrium contracts in labor.

test.q: Which uterine layer is made of smooth muscle and contracts during labor?
test.why: The myometrium is the thick smooth muscle layer that contracts in labor under the influence of oxytocin.

whyNot.0: The endometrium is the inner lining where implantation occurs.
whyNot.1: The perimetrium is the thin outer covering.
whyNot.3: The cervix is the lower neck of the uterus, not one of its wall layers.

explain.body: Starts before birth; primary oocytes pause in prophase I until puberty. Meiosis I finishes just before ovulation (secondary oocyte + polar body); meiosis II finishes only if fertilized.

test.q: At ovulation, the cell released from the ovary is a
test.why: Meiosis I finishes just before ovulation, so a secondary oocyte (with a first polar body) is released.

whyNot.0: Primary oocytes complete meiosis I before ovulation, so the released cell is no longer primary.
whyNot.2: The ovum forms only after meiosis II, which needs fertilization.
whyNot.3: The polar body is a small by-product of meiosis I, not the cell that can be fertilized.

explain.body: FSH grows follicles; follicles make estrogen; high estrogen triggers the LH surge; LH causes ovulation; the corpus luteum secretes progesterone.

test.q: During the follicular phase, which hormone stimulates ovarian follicles to grow?
test.why: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) from the anterior pituitary drives follicle growth.

whyNot.1: LH surges at mid-cycle to trigger ovulation rather than to grow follicles.
whyNot.2: Progesterone dominates the luteal phase, after ovulation.
whyNot.3: hCG is made only after implantation in a pregnancy.

explain.body: Zygote, cleavage, morula, blastocyst, implantation (about 6-7 days), embryo (to week 8), fetus (week 9 to birth). hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive.

test.q: Which sequence of early human development is correct?
test.why: The zygote divides (cleavage) into a morula, which becomes a blastocyst that implants; it is an embryo to week 8, then a fetus.

whyNot.0: The morula comes before the blastocyst.
whyNot.1: The zygote is the first cell, formed at fertilization, so it comes before the morula.
whyNot.2: The embryo stage (to week 8) comes before the fetal stage.
